questions.stem: Which of the following pair regarding vasopressin is incorrect?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) V4-CNS

 

Vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone, ADH) acts via three main receptor types, V1, V2, and V3. There is no V4 receptor in the body, making option D incorrect.

 

Vasopressin Receptors and Their Functions:

 

  1. V1 Receptors (V1a and V1b) – Located on vascular smooth muscles
    • Mechanism: Acts via IP3-DAG pathway, leading to an increase in intracellular calcium (Ca²⁺).
    • Function: Causes vasoconstriction, increasing blood pressure.
    • Correct Pair → Option A
  2. V2 Receptors – Located in the distal collecting ducts of the kidney
    • Mechanism: Works via cAMP-dependent pathway, stimulating Aquaporin-2 (AQP-2) insertion into the apical membrane.
    • Function: Increases water reabsorption, thereby concentrating urine and regulating body fluid balance.
    • Correct Pair → Option B
  3. V3 Receptors – Located in the anterior pituitary (corticotrophs)
    • Mechanism: Works via IP3-DAG pathway, stimulating the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).
    • Function: Regulates ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary, linking vasopressin to the stress response.
    • Correct Pair → Option C
  4. V4 Receptors – Do Not Exist
    • There is no V4 receptor in the vasopressin receptor classification.
    • The CNS does have vasopressin activity, but it is mediated by V1 and V3 receptors, not a separate V4 receptor.

 

Option D (V4 - CNS) is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vasopressin (ADH) acts via V1 (vascular smooth muscle), V2 (renal collecting ducts), and V3 (anterior pituitary) receptors. There is no V4 receptor, making option D incorrect.

questions.stem: All use cAMP as second messenger except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Prolactin

 

Prolactin does not use cAMP as a second messenger. Instead, it acts via the JAK-STAT (Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription) pathway, which is a direct signaling mechanism associated with cytokines and growth factors. This pathway allows prolactin to regulate milk production and other physiological functions without the involvement of cAMP.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Corticotropin: Uses cAMP as a second messenger, activating steroidogenesis in the adrenal cortex.

 

Option B. Dopamine: Functions through cAMP in many cases, especially through D1 receptors.

 

Option C. Glucagon: Directly uses cAMP for its metabolic effects, particularly in glucose metabolism.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Prolactin does not use cAMP as a second messenger; instead, it operates through the JAK-STAT pathway, distinguishing it from many other hormones that rely on GPCR and cAMP signaling.

questions.stem: Statement A: The S cells of the pancreatic islets are associated with the secretion of somatostatin Statement B: Glucagon will be secreted from the gamma cells of the endocrine pancreas Which of the following is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The statement A is true, the statement B is false

options.label: B
options.text: The statement A is false, the statement B is true

options.label: C
options.text: Both the statements A and B are true

options.label: D
options.text: Both the statements A and B are false

questions.answerText: Both the statements A and B are false
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Both the statements A and B are false

 

  • Statement A is false: The S cells do not secrete somatostatin. Instead, delta (D) cells of the pancreatic islets are responsible for somatostatin secretion. S cells are actually found in the duodenum and secrete secretin, which plays a role in regulating pancreatic and biliary secretions.
  • Statement B is false: Glucagon is not secreted by gamma cells. Instead, it is released by alpha (A) cells of the endocrine pancreas, which help regulate blood glucose levels by stimulating glycogen breakdown in the liver. Gamma cells, on the other hand, produce pancreatic polypeptide, which is involved in the regulation of pancreatic secretions and gastrointestinal motility.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Delta (D) cells of the pancreas secrete somatostatin.
  • S cells of the duodenum secrete secretin.
  • Alpha (A) cells of the pancreas secrete glucagon, while gamma (Γ) cells secrete pancreatic polypeptide.

questions.stem: Which of the following will decrease the secretion of insulin? HypokalemiaAcetylcholine GlucagonFasting
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1, 4

 

1. Hypokalemia (Low potassium levels): Insulin secretion is dependent on potassium levels. In hypokalemia, potassium efflux increases, leading to hyperpolarization of beta cells in the pancreas. This prevents the depolarization necessary for calcium influx, which is required for insulin release. Thus, hypokalemia decreases insulin secretion.

 

4. Fasting: When fasting, blood glucose levels are low, leading to decreased stimulation of GLUT2 receptors on pancreatic beta cells. As a result, ATP levels inside the cells do not increase significantly, preventing ATP-sensitive potassium channel closure and calcium influx, leading to reduced insulin secretion.

 

Other Options:

 

2. Acetylcholine: Incorrect: Acetylcholine is a parasympathetic activator that stimulates insulin release. It enhances the activity of pancreatic beta cells, increasing insulin secretion.

 

3. Glucagon: Incorrect: Although glucagon increases blood glucose, it also indirectly stimulates insulin release as a counter-regulatory mechanism to prevent excessive hyperglycemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hypokalemia and fasting decrease insulin secretion.
  • Acetylcholine (parasympathetic stimulation) and glucagon increase insulin secretion.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with hematemesis has heart- burn and stomach pain. An endoscopy shows inflammation involving the gastric body and antrum as well as a small gastric ulcer. Biopsies were positive for H. pylori. H. pylori damages the gastric mucosa primarily by increasing mucosal levels of which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ammonium 

 

Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa, primarily in the antrum, and causes gastritis, peptic ulcers, and in some cases, gastric malignancies.

 

The primary mechanism by which H. pylori damages the gastric mucosa is through the production of urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonia (NH₃) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). Ammonia forms ammonium (NH₄⁺) in the acidic stomach environment. This:

 

  • Increases local alkalinity, which disrupts the protective mucus layer.
  • Induces inflammation and immune response, leading to mucosal damage.
  • Damages gastric epithelial cells, leading to ulcer formation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Bile salts: Bile salts may contribute to gastric irritation but are not a primary factor in H. pylori-induced damage. H. pylori primarily disrupts the mucosal barrier through urease activity.

 

Option C. Gastrin: H. pylori infection, particularly in the antrum, can increase gastrin levels by inhibiting somatostatin-secreting D cells. However, the primary cause of mucosal damage is due to ammonium toxicity and inflammation.

 

Option D. NSAIDs: NSAIDs can cause gastric ulcers by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, which is essential for mucosal protection. However, NSAIDs are not the primary factor in H. pylori-induced gastric damage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

H. pylori damages the gastric mucosa primarily by producing urease, which increases ammonium levels. This disrupts the mucosal barrier, leading to inflammation and ulcer formation.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old female came to the OPD for follow up of vitamin B12 deficiency anemia which is developed post gastrectomy. Intrinsic factors protect the vitamin B12 from degradation in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Small intestine

 

Intrinsic factor (IF) is a glycoprotein secreted by parietal cells of the stomach. Its primary role is to bind to vitamin B12 in the small intestine, preventing its degradation and allowing for absorption in the terminal ileum.

 

  • In the small intestine, pancreatic proteases degrade haptocorrin, allowing intrinsic factor to bind vitamin B12 in the duodenum (D2 region). This complex protects B12 from degradation and facilitates its absorption in the terminal ileum.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Salivary gland: The salivary glands produce haptocorrin (R-protein), which initially binds vitamin B12 but does not provide long-term protection.

 

Option B. Stomach: The stomach secretes intrinsic factor, but vitamin B12 is still bound to haptocorrin at this stage and is not yet protected by intrinsic factor.

 

Option D. Large intestine: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum, and the large intestine plays no role in protecting it from degradation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Intrinsic factor protects vitamin B12 in the small intestine, particularly in the duodenum, by forming a complex that prevents degradation and allows for absorption in the terminal ileum.

questions.stem: The migrating motor complex in humans:

options.label: A
options.text: Occurs only in the small intestine

options.label: B
options.text: Requires an intact intrinsic nervous system for coordinated propagation

options.label: C
options.text: Is the result of food-mediated distension of the small intestine

options.label: D
options.text: Mixes intestinal contents with bile and the digestive enzymes

questions.answerText: Requires an intact intrinsic nervous system for coordinated propagation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Requires an intact intrinsic nervous system for coordinated propagation

 

The Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) is a cyclic, recurrent wave of peristaltic contractions that occurs during the interdigestive phase (between meals) to clear residual undigested material from the stomach and small intestine. It is often referred to as the “sweeper” or “broomstick” of the GIT because it helps in clearing leftover food particles and bacteria.

 

  • The MMC is controlled by the intrinsic nervous system, particularly the myenteric plexus (part of the enteric nervous system), which coordinates smooth muscle contraction. Therefore, an intact intrinsic nervous system is necessary for MMC propagation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Occurs only in the small intestine: MMC starts in the stomach and propagates through the small intestine to the terminal ileum.

 

Option C. Is the result of food-mediated distension of the small intestine: MMC occurs in the fasting state, not in response to food. It ceases when food is ingested.

 

Option D. Mixes intestinal contents with bile and digestive enzymes: MMC functions between meals to clear the GIT, not to mix food with bile or enzymes, which occurs during digestion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) is a cyclic peristaltic movement that occurs between meals to clear residual food and bacteria from the stomach and small intestine. It requires an intact intrinsic nervous system (myenteric plexus) for coordination and is not triggered by food ingestion.

questions.stem: Most common cause of iron deficiency anemia is lack of dietary intake of iron. Iron is transported from enterocyte to capillary through:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ferroprotein

 

Iron absorption occurs in the duodenum and proximal jejunum through a well-regulated process:

 

  1. Divalent Metal Transporter 1 (DMT1) allows iron absorption from the intestinal lumen into enterocytes.
  2. Once inside the enterocyte, iron is either:
    • Stored as ferritin, or
    • Transported into the bloodstream via ferroportin.
  3. Ferroportin is the only known iron exporter, allowing iron to pass from enterocytes into the capillary.
  4. After leaving the enterocyte, hephaestin converts Fe²⁺ into Fe³⁺, enabling it to bind to transferrin, which transports it in the bloodstream.
  5. Hepcidin, a regulatory hormone, inhibits ferroportin when iron levels are high, reducing iron absorption.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. GLUT: GLUT (Glucose Transporter) proteins are involved in glucose transport, not iron transport.

 

Option B. DMT2: No such transporter as DMT2 exists in the context of iron absorption. The correct transporter for iron uptake from the lumen is DMT1.

 

Option D. DMT1: DMT1 is responsible for absorbing iron from the intestinal lumen into the enterocyte, but the question specifically asks about transport from the enterocyte to the capillary, which is done by ferroportin.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Iron is transported from the intestinal lumen to the enterocyte by DMT1, but it is exported from the enterocyte to the capillary via ferroportin.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male comes to OPD with complain of weight loss despite overeating, continuous thirst sensation and increased urinary frequency. The physician advised investigation one of which was glucose tolerance test. Glucose is absorbed in intestine by?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Secondary active transport

 

Glucose absorption in the small intestine primarily occurs via the Sodium-Glucose Linked Transporter 1 (SGLT1), which is an example of secondary active transport.

 

  • SGLT1 is located in the brush border of intestinal enterocytes (mainly in the small intestine).
  • It transports glucose and sodium (Na⁺) together into the enterocyte using the sodium concentration gradient created by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump on the basolateral side.
  • Once inside the enterocyte, glucose exits into the bloodstream via facilitated diffusion using the GLUT2 transporter.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Facilitated diffusion: GLUT2 helps in glucose transport from enterocytes to capillaries, but glucose absorption from the intestinal lumen requires active transport.

 

Option C. Simple diffusion: Glucose is a polar molecule and cannot cross the lipid bilayer passively; it requires specific transporters.

 

Option D. Primary active transport: This involves the direct use of ATP (e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase), but glucose absorption occurs via secondary active transport using the sodium gradient, not direct ATP hydrolysis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by SGLT1 via secondary active transport, which relies on the sodium gradient maintained by Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase.

questions.stem: A 34-year male came to OPD with complain of heartburn from last 2 months, he further says the acidity increases after eating so he developed anorexia. Which one of the following does not increase secretion of gastric acid?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Secretin

 

Secretin is a hormone released by S cells in the duodenum in response to acidic chyme. It plays a crucial role in neutralizing stomach acid by:

 

  • Inhibiting gastrin release, thereby reducing gastric acid secretion.
  • Stimulating bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) secretion from the pancreas, which helps neutralize acid in the duodenum.
  • Reducing gastric motility, preventing excessive acid influx into the duodenum.

 

Since secretin counteracts acid secretion, it is the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Acetylcholine (ACh): Increases gastric acid secretion by binding to M3 muscarinic receptors on parietal cells, stimulating hydrogen ion (H⁺) secretion.

 

Option C. Histamine: Released by enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells, histamine binds to H₂ receptors on parietal cells, stimulating acid secretion.

 

Option D. Gastrin: Released by G cells in the stomach, gastrin binds to CCK2 (cholecystokinin B) receptors on parietal cells, directly stimulating acid secretion and also increasing histamine release from ECL cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Secretin inhibits gastric acid secretion by stimulating bicarbonate secretion and reducing gastrin release, whereas acetylcholine, histamine, and gastrin increase acid secretion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following does not have a Na+ I- transporter?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pituitary

 

The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is a specialized transporter that facilitates the active uptake of iodide (I⁻) along with sodium (Na⁺) into certain tissues where iodide is essential for biological functions.

 

The Na⁺/I⁻ transporter is present in:

 

  • Thyroid gland – For iodide uptake, which is required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones (T3 & T4).
  • Salivary glands – Uptakes iodide, but it is not used for hormone synthesis.
  • Placenta – Expresses NIS to ensure iodine supply to the developing fetus.
  • Mammary glands (during lactation) – Helps provide iodine in breast milk to support neonatal thyroid function.

 

However, the pituitary gland does not express the Na⁺/I⁻ symporter. While the pituitary regulates thyroid function through TSH (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone), it does not require direct iodide transport for its function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Salivary Gland: Contains NIS and uptakes iodide but does not use it for hormone synthesis.


Option C. Placenta: Expresses NIS to ensure iodine supply to the fetus for proper thyroid development.


Option D. Thyroid: The primary organ where iodide uptake occurs for the synthesis of thyroid hormones.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Na⁺/I⁻ symporter (NIS) is present in the thyroid, salivary glands, placenta, and mammary glands, but not in the pituitary gland.

questions.stem: The hypothalamus and fat tissues also play an important role in the regulation of energy metabolism Leptin acts by increasing the activity of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Alpha MSH

 

Leptin is a hormone primarily produced by adipose tissue (fat cells) that plays a crucial role in energy homeostasis and appetite regulation by acting on the hypothalamus.

 

  • Leptin stimulates α-MSH (Alpha Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone) by activating POMC (Pro-opiomelanocortin) neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
  • α-MSH binds to melanocortin receptors (MC4R), leading to decreased appetite and increased energy expenditure, promoting satiety.

 

Leptin also inhibits orexigenic (hunger-promoting) neuropeptides:

 

  • AgRP (Agouti-related peptide) → An antagonist of MC4R that promotes hunger.
  • Neuropeptide Y (NPY) → A potent appetite stimulant.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. AgRP: Leptin inhibits AgRP, which normally increases food intake by blocking MC4R.

 

Option B. Neuropeptide Y (NPY): Leptin inhibits NPY, which is one of the strongest hunger-stimulating neuropeptides in the hypothalamus.

 

Option D. Ghrelin: Ghrelin is secreted by the stomach and promotes hunger. Leptin does not directly increase ghrelin activity; instead, it acts as an antagonist by reducing hunger signals.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Leptin increases the activity of α-MSH, which promotes satiety and reduces food intake. At the same time, it inhibits AgRP and Neuropeptide Y, which are responsible for increasing hunger.

questions.stem: The morning after a rock concert, a 20-year-old college student notices difficulty hearing his professor during lecture. The physician at the Student Health Center suspects possible damage to his hair cells by the loud music. Depolarization of the hair cells in the cochlea is caused primarily by the flow of which of the following?

options.label: C
options.text: Cl– out of the hair cell

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) K+ into the hair cell 

 

Hair cells in the cochlea play a crucial role in mechanotransduction, converting sound vibrations into electrical signals. These cells have stereocilia, which are immersed in the endolymph, a potassium-rich fluid secreted by the stria vascularis.

 

  • When sound waves cause the basilar membrane to move, the stereocilia bend.
  • This bending opens mechanically gated potassium (K⁺) channels at the tips of the stereocilia, allowing K⁺ ions to enter from the endolymph.
  • Since K⁺ is positively charged, its influx leads to depolarization of the hair cell.
  • Depolarization then opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, leading to neurotransmitter release and signal transmission to the auditory nerve.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Na⁺ into the hair cell: Unlike many excitable cells that depolarize via Na⁺ influx, hair cells depolarize via K⁺ influx, as endolymph has a high K⁺ concentration.

 

Option C. Cl⁻ out of the hair cell: Chloride ions do not play a major role in hair cell depolarization.

 

Option D. Ca²⁺ into the hair cell: Calcium influx occurs after depolarization, leading to neurotransmitter release, but it is not the primary cause of depolarization.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hair cells in the cochlea depolarize due to K⁺ influx from the potassium-rich endolymph, which is secreted by the stria vascularis. This potassium influx occurs through mechanically gated channels in the stereocilia, initiating the hearing signal.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old patient recovers from COVID 19 infection, but still complains of no improvement in Smell and taste sensation. Bitter taste is mediated by action of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) G protein

 

Taste sensation is primarily classified into two types of receptor mechanisms:

 

  1. Ionotropic receptors (Direct channel activation) – Involve direct ion flow through channels, responsible for:
    • Salty (Na⁺ channels)
    • Sour (H⁺ channels)
  2. Metabotropic receptors (GPCR pathway activation) – Involve G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), responsible for:
    • Bitter (T2R receptors) → Activates G protein (Gustducin)
    • Sweet (T1R2/T1R3 receptors)
    • Umami (T1R1/T1R3 receptors)

 

Bitter taste is mediated by G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), specifically gustducin, which activates a secondary messenger cascade that leads to depolarization and taste perception.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Guanylyl cyclase: Incorrect, as it is primarily involved in phototransduction in the retina, not taste sensation.

 

Option C. Tyrosine kinase: Incorrect, as tyrosine kinase receptors are involved in growth factor signaling (e.g., insulin receptors), not taste perception.

 

Option D. Epithelial Na channel (ENaC): Incorrect, as ENaC is responsible for salt taste detection, not bitter taste.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Bitter taste is detected through G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), specifically T2R receptors that activate gustducin, leading to taste signal transduction.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency room after a traffic accident causing a traumatic brain injury. Within several hours he begins eating objects such as paper, is unable to maintain attention, and displays increased sexual activity. He is diagnosed with Kluver-Bucy syndrome. A diagnostic MRI is ordered to confirm bilateral lesions of which of the following regions of the brain?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Temporal lobe

 

Klüver-Bucy syndrome results from bilateral lesions of the anterior temporal lobes, particularly the amygdala. This condition is characterized by:

 

  • Hyperorality – Compulsive eating or chewing of objects.
  • Hypermetamorphosis – Excessive curiosity, inability to focus attention, and a tendency to explore objects indiscriminately.
  • Hypersexuality – Increased sexual behaviors, often inappropriate.
  • Emotional blunting – Lack of fear and diminished emotional responses.
  • Visual agnosia – Inability to recognize objects despite intact vision.

 

The temporal lobe, especially the amygdala, is involved in regulating emotions, fear response, and behavioral inhibition. When both amygdalae are damaged, Klüver-Bucy syndrome develops.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Hypothalamus: The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst, and autonomic functions but is not primarily responsible for Klüver-Bucy syndrome.

 

Option C. Olfactory lobe: While the olfactory bulb is involved in the sense of smell, it does not cause hyperorality, hypersexuality, or visual agnosia when damaged.

 

Option D. Hippocampus: The hippocampus is critical for memory formation, and its damage leads to anterograde amnesia, not the behavioral changes seen in Klüver-Bucy syndrome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Klüver-Bucy syndrome is caused by bilateral lesions of the temporal lobe, particularly the amygdala, and is characterized by hyperorality, hypermetamorphosis, hypersexuality, and emotional blunting.

questions.stemHtml: In the diagram given below what are A & B?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Kinesin and dynein

 

The diagram represents axonal transport, which occurs along microtubules using motor proteins:

 

  1. A (Kinesin) – Anterograde transport (from the cell body to the axon terminal)
    • Kinesin is a microtubule-associated motor protein that moves vesicles, organelles, and neurotransmitters toward the axon terminal (positive end of the microtubule).
    • This movement is crucial for synaptic transmission and cell maintenance.
  2. B (Dynein) – Retrograde transport (from the axon terminal back to the cell body)
    • Dynein moves recycled vesicles, growth factors, and sometimes harmful agents like viruses/toxins back to the cell body (negative end of the microtubule).
    • This process allows for recycling of cellular components and communication with the nucleus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Dynein and Kinesin: Incorrect because A represents anterograde transport (Kinesin) and B represents retrograde transport (Dynein).

 

Option C. Calmodulin and SNARE: These are involved in calcium signaling and vesicle fusion, not axonal transport.

 

Option D. SNARE and Calmodulin: SNARE proteins assist in synaptic vesicle docking and fusion, not in intracellular transport.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Kinesin mediates anterograde transport (towards the axon terminal).
  • Dynein mediates retrograde transport (back to the cell body).
  • Axonal transport is essential for neuronal function, synaptic transmission, and cellular maintenance.

questions.stem: In skin the somatosensory receptors work as a transducer, which convert various types of sensation into electrical energy and sent the signals to the brain. One of them is onion shaped corpuscles present in dermis. It detects which one of the following properties?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Vibration

 

The onion-shaped corpuscles in the dermis refer to Pacinian corpuscles, which are specialized mechanoreceptors responsible for detecting:

 

  • Deep pressure
  • High-frequency vibration (250–350 Hz)

 

Key features of Pacinian corpuscles:

 

  • They are rapidly adapting receptors, meaning they respond quickly to changes in pressure but stop firing if the stimulus is continuous.
  • Their lamellar (onion-like) structure helps in sensing vibration and deep pressure changes rather than constant pressure.
  • Located in deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue, they are essential for perceiving textures and detecting vibrational stimuli in objects.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Pain: Detected by free nerve endings (nociceptors), not Pacinian corpuscles.

 

Option C. Fine touch: Detected by Merkel cells and Meissner’s corpuscles, which are found in the epidermis and dermal papillae, respectively.

 

Option D. Temperature: Detected by thermoreceptors (cold and warm receptors), which transmit signals via Aδ and C fibers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pacinian corpuscles (onion-shaped) are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors that detect deep pressure and high-frequency vibrations.

questions.stem: A 32-year male patient comes to the OPD with the complain of diffuse pain in abdomen from last 3 hours. While history taking he tells the attending physician that he ate street food last night. This sensation is transmitted by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C Fibers

 

Pain perception is mediated by two types of nerve fibers:

 

  1. A delta fibers → Carry sharp, localized, pricking pain (also known as "good pain")
    • Fast conduction due to myelination
    • Causes withdrawal reflex to protect the body from harmful stimuli
  2. C fibers → Carry dull, burning, diffuse, and slow pain (also called "bad pain")
    • Unmyelinated, leading to slow conduction
    • Associated with visceral pain, nausea, vomiting, and autonomic symptoms

 

Since this patient has diffuse abdominal pain, it is classified as visceral pain, which is transmitted primarily by C fibers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A delta fibers: Transmit sharp, well-localized pain, such as a pinprick or cut, but not diffuse visceral pain.

 

Option B. A alpha fibers: Involved in motor functions and proprioception, not pain transmission.

 

Option D. B fibers: Involved in autonomic functions, including preganglionic sympathetic nerve transmission, but not pain perception.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Visceral pain (diffuse, dull, poorly localized pain) is transmitted by unmyelinated C fibers, whereas sharp, localized pain is carried by A delta fibers.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentence is incorrect related to perception of sensory stimuli related to pain:

options.label: A
options.text: Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated pain response to an innocuous stimulus

options.label: B
options.text: Allodynia is a sensation of pain in response to an innocuous stimulus

options.label: C
options.text: Causalgia is a type of neuropathic pain

questions.answerText: Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated pain response to an innocuous stimulus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated pain response to an innocuous stimulus

 

  • Hyperalgesia – It refers to an exaggerated pain response to a noxious (harmful) stimulus, not an innocuous (harmless) stimulus. This occurs due to sensitization of nociceptors, often seen in inflammatory pain or nerve damage. The incorrect statement in the question is that hyperalgesia is triggered by an innocuous stimulus—this is actually the definition of allodynia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Allodynia is a sensation of pain in response to an innocuous stimulus: Correct. Defined as pain in response to an innocuous (harmless) stimulus, such as light touch causing severe pain. This can occur due to nerve injury, postherpetic neuralgia, or central sensitization.

 

Option C. Causalgia is a type of neuropathic pain: Correct. A form of neuropathic pain, usually associated with complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS Type II). It presents as severe, persistent burning pain following nerve injury.

 

Option D. None of the above: Incorrect, since statement A is false.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hyperalgesia = Exaggerated pain response to a noxious (harmful) stimulus.
  • Allodynia = Pain in response to a non-noxious (harmless) stimulus.
  • Causalgia = A type of neuropathic pain seen in nerve injuries.

questions.stem: A 32-year male was working in a factory came to emergency with neurological deficit after an unfortunate accident. After thorough clinical examination and evaluation of patient’s symptoms the physician suspecting a syndrome where hemi-section of a spinal cord occurs. In this abnormality which of the following occurs at the level of the lesion:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) LMN paralysis

 

This case describes Brown-Séquard syndrome, a condition caused by hemisection of the spinal cord. The effects of this syndrome vary based on whether they occur at the level of the lesion or below it:

 

  • At the level of the lesion:
    • Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) paralysis occurs due to damage to the anterior horn cells (alpha and gamma motor neurons).
    • There is also complete sensory loss at the lesion level, as the dorsal root neurons are affected.
  • Below the level of the lesion:
    • Ipsilateral (same side) UMN paralysis due to corticospinal tract damage, as these fibers have already crossed at the medulla.
    • Ipsilateral fine touch, vibration, and proprioception loss due to dorsal column involvement (gracile and cuneate tracts).
    • Contralateral (opposite side) pain and temperature loss due to spinothalamic tract damage, which crosses 2-3 segments above its entry point.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Contralateral pain loss: This occurs below the lesion, not at the lesion level, due to spinothalamic tract damage.

 

Option B. Contralateral fine touch loss: Incorrect, because the dorsal column crosses at the medulla, so fine touch is lost ipsilaterally below the lesion, not contralaterally.

 

Option C. UMN paralysis: Upper Motor Neuron signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity) appear below the lesion, while LMN paralysis occurs at the lesion level.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In Brown-Séquard syndrome:

 

  • At the lesion level → LMN paralysis and total sensory loss.
  • Below the lesion → Ipsilateral UMN paralysis, ipsilateral fine touch loss, and contralateral pain and temperature loss.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old male is evaluated by a physiatrist after a stroke. The patient is observed to suffer from dysmetria, ataxia, and an intention tremor. These neurological signs are most likely related to a lesion within which of the following regions of the brain?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cerebellum

 

The cerebellum plays a critical role in coordinating voluntary movements, maintaining balance, and fine-tuning motor control. Lesions in the cerebellum lead to motor incoordination without muscle weakness, presenting as:

 

  • Ataxia – Uncoordinated, unsteady movements due to impaired balance and posture control.
  • Dysmetria – Inability to judge distances properly, leading to overshooting (hypermetria) or undershooting (hypometria) when reaching for an object.
  • Intention tremor – Tremors that occur during voluntary movement (e.g., when trying to touch a target), worsening as the movement progresses.
  • Adiadochokinesia – Inability to perform rapid alternating movements (e.g., rapid pronation and supination of the hands).
  • Rebound phenomenon – Difficulty controlling muscle contraction after resistance is removed, leading to exaggerated movement.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Medulla: The medulla controls autonomic functions like respiration and cardiovascular regulation. Medullary lesions would cause dysphagia, respiratory distress, and autonomic dysfunction, not ataxia and intention tremors.

 

Option C. Cortical motor strip: The primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus) controls voluntary movement, and damage leads to muscle weakness or paralysis, not ataxia or intention tremors.

 

Option D. Basal ganglia: The basal ganglia are responsible for movement initiation and regulation, with lesions leading to Parkinsonian symptoms (resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity) or hyperkinetic disorders like Huntington’s disease. Basal ganglia dysfunction does not cause intention tremor or dysmetria.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lesions in the cerebellum cause ataxia, dysmetria, and intention tremors, affecting motor coordination without causing muscle weakness.

questions.stem: While studying the stimulus given at different time interval and their responses Pavlov performed various experiment on dogs, in Pavlov’s famous experiment the dog shows which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Conditional response

 

Pavlov’s classical conditioning experiment involved pairing a neutral stimulus (bell) with an unconditioned stimulus (food). Over time, the dog learned to associate the bell with food and would salivate upon hearing the bell, even when no food was presented.

 

  • Initially, food (unconditioned stimulus, US) naturally caused salivation (unconditioned response, UR).
  • The bell (neutral stimulus, NS) alone did not cause salivation.
  • After repeated pairings of the bell with food, the bell became a conditioned stimulus (CS), and the dog began salivating in response to the bell alone.
  • This learned response is called a conditioned response (CR).

 

Thus, in Pavlov’s experiment, the dog showed a conditioned response (CR) when salivating in response to the bell alone.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Unconditioned response: This refers to salivation in response to food (natural reflex), not the learned response to the bell.

 

Option C. Procedural memory: This involves skills and motor learning (e.g., riding a bike), not classical conditioning.

 

Option D. Familiarity: This refers to recognizing previously encountered stimuli, which is unrelated to Pavlov’s conditioning.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Classical conditioning involves learning through association, where a neutral stimulus (bell) becomes a conditioned stimulus after repeated pairings with an unconditioned stimulus (food), leading to a conditioned response (salivation to the bell alone).

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman eats a high carbohydrate meal. Her plasma glucose concentration rises, and this results in increased insulin secretion from the pancreatic islet cells. Glucose mediated insulin release is mediated through:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) ATP sensitive K+ channels

 

Glucose-mediated insulin release from pancreatic beta cells occurs through the following mechanism:

 

  1. Glucose uptake – Glucose enters pancreatic β-cells via GLUT2 (glucose transporter 2), which is insulin-independent.
  2. Glycolysis and ATP production – The glucose is metabolized to generate ATP through glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation.
  3. ATP-sensitive K⁺ channel closure – The increased ATP closes ATP-sensitive potassium (K⁺) channels, leading to membrane depolarization.
  4. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel activation – The depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, allowing Ca²⁺ influx into the cell.
  5. Insulin exocytosis – The increased intracellular Ca²⁺ triggers insulin secretion from storage vesicles.

 

Thus, the ATP-sensitive K⁺ channel is the key regulator of glucose-stimulated insulin release.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. cAMP: Although cAMP plays a role in hormone-stimulated insulin secretion (e.g., GLP-1, GIP signaling), it is not the primary mediator of glucose-induced insulin release.

 

Option C. Carrier modulators: Carrier proteins facilitate glucose transport but do not directly trigger insulin release.

 

Option D. Receptor phosphorylation: Insulin signaling involves receptor phosphorylation, but insulin secretion does not.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glucose-mediated insulin secretion occurs via ATP-sensitive K⁺ channel closure, leading to membrane depolarization, Ca²⁺ influx, and insulin exocytosis from pancreatic β-cells.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman is referred to a neurologist by her family physician because of a recent loss of initiative, lethargy, memory problems, and a loss of vision. She is diagnosed with primary hypothyroidism and referred to an endocrinologist for treatment of her thyroid problem. All the following are functions of thyroid cells except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Synthesize thyroid hormones

 

The synthesis of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) does not occur inside thyroid follicular cells but in the colloid.

 

  • Within follicular cells, thyroglobulin is synthesized and secreted into the colloid, where it undergoes iodination and coupling reactions to form T3 and T4.
  • The actual formation of thyroid hormones occurs in the colloid space, facilitated by thyroid peroxidase (TPO), which catalyzes the oxidation of iodide, organification, and coupling reactions.
  • Since T3 and T4 synthesis occurs outside the follicular cells, they do not directly synthesize thyroid hormones, making this the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Collect and transport iodine: Thyroid follicular cells actively transport iodine using the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) and release it into the colloid via pendrin protein.

 

Option B. Synthesize thyroglobulin: Follicular cells produce thyroglobulin, a precursor required for thyroid hormone synthesis.

 

Option C. Secrete thyroid hormones: After processing, T3 and T4 are released from follicular cells into the bloodstream upon TSH stimulation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The synthesis of T3 and T4 occurs in the colloid, not inside thyroid follicular cells. However, thyroid follicular cells collect iodine, synthesize thyroglobulin, and secrete hormones into circulation.

questions.stem: Which of the following regarding actions on plasma Ca++ and PO4- is true:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) PTH : ↑ Ca²⁺, ↓ PO₄³⁻

 

The regulation of calcium (Ca²⁺) and phosphate (PO₄³⁻) homeostasis is primarily controlled by parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcitonin, and 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (1,25 DHCC or active Vitamin D3).

 

  • Parathyroid Hormone (PTH):
    • Increases Ca²⁺ levels by stimulating bone resorption, increasing renal calcium reabsorption, and enhancing intestinal calcium absorption (via activation of vitamin D).
    • Decreases PO₄³⁻ levels by inhibiting phosphate reabsorption in the kidneys, leading to increased phosphate excretion.
    • Thus, PTH increases plasma Ca²⁺ and decreases PO₄³⁻, making Option C correct.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 1,25 DHCC (Active Vitamin D3): ↑ Ca²⁺, ↓ PO₄³⁻: Incorrect. Vitamin D (1,25-DHCC) increases both Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ absorption from the intestines. It does not decrease phosphate levels.

 

Option B. Calcitonin: ↓ Ca²⁺, ↑ PO₄³⁻: Incorrect. Calcitonin lowers Ca²⁺ and phosphate levels by inhibiting bone resorption. However, it has minimal effect on phosphate levels in plasma.

 

Option D. None of the above: Incorrect, since Option C is correct.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • PTH increases Ca²⁺ and decreases PO₄³⁻ by enhancing bone resorption and inhibiting phosphate reabsorption in the kidney.
  • 1,25-DHCC (Vitamin D3) increases both Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ absorption in the intestines.
  • Calcitonin lowers both Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ by inhibiting bone resorption.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old obese female with type 2 DM and hypertension presents to discuss an elevated level of prolactin. She complained of galactorrhoea and no menses for two years. The secretion of this hormone is controlled by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Dopamine

 

Prolactin is secreted by lactotroph cells of the anterior pituitary and is an acidophilic hormone. It plays a role in milk production (lactation) and reproductive function regulation.

 

  • Dopamine acts as Prolactin Inhibitory Factor (PIF) and is released from the hypothalamus, binding to D2 receptors on lactotroph cells, thereby inhibiting prolactin secretion.
  • If dopamine levels decrease due to hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction, prolactin secretion increases, leading to galactorrhea and menstrual irregularities (amenorrhea).
  • Hyperprolactinemia is commonly caused by a pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma), hypothalamic dysfunction, or medications (e.g., antipsychotics that block dopamine receptors).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Serotonin: Does not have a direct regulatory effect on prolactin secretion.

 

Option B. GABA: Acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain but does not primarily regulate prolactin.

 

Option C. Somatostatin: Inhibits growth hormone (GH) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) but does not regulate prolactin secretion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dopamine (Prolactin Inhibitory Factor, PIF) inhibits prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary. A decrease in dopamine leads to hyperprolactinemia, causing galactorrhea and amenorrhea.

questions.stem: Which of the following has a higher concentration in urine after coming through PCT?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Chloride

 

The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) is responsible for the reabsorption of most essential substances from the filtrate back into the bloodstream. The percentage of reabsorption for each substance determines its relative concentration in the urine after passing through the PCT.

 

  • Chloride (C) – Unlike glucose and amino acids, only about 60-65% of chloride (Cl⁻) is reabsorbed in the PCT, meaning a significant portion (~35-40%) remains in the urine after passing through the PCT. This makes chloride the correct answer, as it has the highest concentration in the urine after the PCT.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glucose: Completely reabsorbed in the PCT, so it should not appear in urine under normal conditions.

 

Option B. Amino acids: Also fully reabsorbed in the PCT.

 

Option D. Bicarbonate: Around 75-80% of bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) is reabsorbed in the PCT, leaving only a small fraction in the urine. Since bicarbonate plays a crucial role in acid-base balance, its reabsorption is tightly regulated.

 

Educational Objective:

 

After passing through the PCT, chloride (Cl⁻) has the highest concentration in the urine, as it is only partially reabsorbed (~60-65%), whereas glucose and amino acids are completely reabsorbed, and bicarbonate is largely reabsorbed (~80%).

questions.stem: Which of the following graphs represent correct relationship between “mean arterial BP” and “plasma vasopressin(pmol/L)” Abscissa= mean arterial BP; Ordinate= plasma vasopressin
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. 

 

The relationship between mean arterial blood pressure (BP) and plasma vasopressin follows an inverse relationship, meaning as mean arterial BP increases, plasma vasopressin decreases. This is because:

 

  • Vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone, ADH) is released primarily in response to low blood pressure or hypovolemia to conserve water and increase blood pressure.
  • When mean arterial BP is low, vasopressin secretion increases, causing water retention and vasoconstriction, which helps restore BP.
  • When mean arterial BP rises, vasopressin secretion decreases, since the body no longer needs to retain water or constrict blood vessels.

 

Graph C correctly represents this inverse relationship, where the ordinate (y-axis) represents plasma vasopressin and the abscissa (x-axis) represents mean arterial BP. The graph shows a declining curve, indicating that as BP increases, vasopressin levels fall.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: This graph shows a linear positive relationship, implying that as BP increases, vasopressin increases. However, this is incorrect because vasopressin secretion actually decreases when BP rises.

 

Option B: This graph shows an exponential increase, suggesting that vasopressin rises sharply with BP, which is incorrect. In reality, vasopressin secretion is suppressed when BP is high.

 

Option D: This graph represents a logarithmic relationship where vasopressin initially increases with BP and then plateaus. However, this does not correctly depict the physiological response, as vasopressin secretion should decrease when BP rises.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Plasma vasopressin secretion is inversely related to mean arterial blood pressure. When BP is low, vasopressin secretion increases to retain water and restore BP. When BP is high, vasopressin secretion decreases to reduce unnecessary water retention and prevent hypertension.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the diluting segment of kidney?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Thick ascending limb of LOH

 

The diluting segment of the nephron refers to the part of the kidney that removes solutes (Na⁺, Cl⁻) from the filtrate but is impermeable to water, leading to a dilution of urine.

 

  • The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (TAL) actively reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ via the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter.
  • It is impermeable to water, meaning water cannot follow the solutes, leading to dilution of the tubular fluid as it ascends toward the distal convoluted tubule (DCT).
  • This segment is critical for generating the medullary concentration gradient required for urine concentration later in the collecting duct under antidiuretic hormone (ADH) influence.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. PCT (Proximal Convoluted Tubule): This segment is highly permeable to water and solutes, leading to isosmotic reabsorption, meaning it does not dilute the urine.

 

Option C. Thin Descending Limb of LOH: This segment is permeable to water but not solutes, causing water reabsorption and urine concentration, not dilution.

 

Option D. Collecting Duct: The permeability of the collecting duct depends on ADH levels. It does not function as a diluting segment; instead, it helps concentrate or dilute the urine based on hydration status.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (TAL) is the primary diluting segment of the kidney because it actively reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ but is impermeable to water, leading to the production of dilute urine.

questions.stem: For the following question, Assertion - Constriction of efferent arteriole can decrease GFR. Reason - More than threefold increase in resistance decreases Renal blood flow& increase in colloid osmotic pressure. Mark the correct option as per the following direction: Select one of the following:

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion and Reasons are independently correct statements, and the Reason is the correct explanation for the Assertion.

options.label: B
options.text: Assertion is independently a correct statement, but the Reasons is independently an incorrect statement.

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion is independently an incorrect statement, but the Reasons is independently a correct statement.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion and Reasons are independently incorrect statements

questions.answerText: Both Assertion and Reasons are independently correct statements, and the Reason is the correct explanation for the Assertion.
questions.solutionHtml:
The effect of efferent arteriole constriction on glomerular filtration rate (GFR) depends on the degree of constriction:

 

  1. Mild to moderate constriction:
    • Increases glomerular hydrostatic pressure, which initially increases GFR.
    • However, renal blood flow (RBF) decreases, leading to a gradual increase in colloid osmotic pressure (oncotic pressure) in the glomerular capillaries.
  2. Severe constriction (more than threefold resistance increase):
    • Significantly reduces renal blood flow, decreasing the availability of plasma to be filtered.
    • The colloid osmotic pressure rises sharply, counteracting the increased hydrostatic pressure.
    • Ultimately, this reduces net filtration pressure (NFP) and decreases GFR.

 

Since both statements are correct and the reason explains the assertion, Option A is the correct answer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mild to moderate constriction of the efferent arteriole increases GFR, but severe constriction leads to a sharp rise in oncotic pressure, reducing GFR due to decreased renal blood flow.

questions.answerText: Motilin – M cells from duodenum and jejunum
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Motilin – M cells from duodenum and jejunum

 

Motilin is not secreted by M cells. Instead, it is secreted by Mo (Motilin-secreting) cells in the duodenum and jejunum.

 

  • M cells are found in Peyer’s patches and are involved in antigen transport and immune function, not hormone secretion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gastrin - G cells from stomach: Correct, gastrin is secreted by G cells in the antrum of the stomach and stimulates gastric acid secretion.

 

Option C. CCK from I cells of duodenum and pancreas: Correct, I cells in the duodenum and jejunum release CCK, which stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.

 

Option D. Secretin from S cells of duodenum and jejunum: Correct, S cells release Secretin, which stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion to neutralize gastric acid.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Motilin is secreted by Mo cells, not M cells, which are involved in immune function rather than hormone secretion.

questions.stem: All the following vessels show Wind Kessel effect except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Radial artery

 

The Windkessel effect refers to the ability of large, elastic arteries to store energy during systole and release it during diastole, ensuring continuous blood flow. This effect is primarily observed in elastic arteries that contain high amounts of elastin fibers, allowing them to stretch and recoil.

 

  • Aorta  and Carotid artery  are large elastic arteries, playing a key role in the Windkessel effect by damping pulsatile flow.
  • Renal artery is also a relatively large artery with some elastic properties.
  • Radial artery is a muscular artery, not an elastic artery, meaning it lacks significant Windkessel function. Muscular arteries primarily regulate blood flow through vasoconstriction and vasodilation rather than elastic recoil.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aorta: A major elastic artery, plays a key role in the Windkessel effect.

 

Option B. Renal artery: Though not as elastic as the aorta, it still has some elastic properties contributing to the Windkessel effect.

 

Option D. Carotid artery: A large elastic artery, contributing to continuous cerebral blood flow via the Windkessel effect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Windkessel effect is present in large elastic arteries (Aorta, Carotid, and Renal arteries) but not in smaller muscular arteries like the Radial artery, which primarily function through vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: Arrange the parts of the Sarcomere from periphery to center. Z line M lineA bandH zone
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1, 3, 4, 2

 

The sarcomere is the structural and functional unit of skeletal muscle, and it consists of several key regions:

 

1. Z Line (Z Disc) – The peripheral boundary of the sarcomere where actin filaments attach.

 

3. A Band – The entire length of the myosin filament, including overlapping actin. This region remains constant in size during contraction.

 

4. H Zone – The central region within the A band where only myosin is present (no overlapping actin). It shortens during contraction.

 

2. M Line – The center of the sarcomere, containing proteins that hold the myosin filaments together.

 

Arrangement from Periphery to Center:

 

1. Z line (outermost)

 

3. A band (contains both actin and myosin)

 

4. H zone (only myosin, no actin overlap)

 

2. M line (innermost, center of myosin filaments)

 

Thus, the correct order is 1 → 3 → 4 → 2, corresponding to Option A.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The sarcomere is organized from the periphery to the center as follows: Z line → A band → H zone → M line.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is the True statement regarding Skeletal muscle? Extracellular Ca2+ is not important for contraction.Ca2+ released mainly from Mitochondria.Ca2+ released from sarcoplasmic reticulum.Voltage gated Ca2+ channels on sarcolemma has no role in EC coupling.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1, 3

 

1. Extracellular Ca²⁺ is not important for skeletal muscle contraction: This is true. Unlike cardiac and smooth muscle, skeletal muscle contraction does not rely on extracellular Ca²⁺. The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is the primary source of Ca²⁺ needed for contraction in skeletal muscle.

 

3. Ca²⁺ released from the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum (SR): This is true. In skeletal muscle, the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the SR releases Ca²⁺ in response to depolarization. This Ca²⁺ binds to troponin C, leading to muscle contraction.

 

Other Options:

 

2. Ca²⁺ released mainly from Mitochondria: This is false. Mitochondria do not serve as the main source of calcium for muscle contraction. Instead, Ca²⁺ is stored and released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).

 

4. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels on the sarcolemma have no role in EC coupling: This is false. While these channels (Dihydropyridine Receptors, DHPR) do not open to allow Ca²⁺ influx, they play a crucial role in activating RyR1 on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which triggers Ca²⁺ release.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Skeletal muscle contraction relies on intracellular Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not extracellular Ca²⁺. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels (DHPR) on the sarcolemma do not allow Ca²⁺ influx but are essential for activating RyR1 and initiating Ca²⁺ release from the SR.

questions.stem: In respiratory tract the Airway pressure is zero at which of the following Lung volume?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) FRC

 

  • Airway pressure is zero when the respiratory system is at equilibrium, meaning no airflow occurs between breaths.
  • This happens at Functional Residual Capacity (FRC), which is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal tidal expiration.
  • At FRC, the inward elastic recoil of the lungs is balanced by the outward recoil of the chest wall, resulting in a zero airway pressure (atmospheric pressure).
  • This equilibrium point is also known as the relaxation volume.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Residual Volume (RV): Incorrect, because at RV, airway pressure is negative, as additional effort is required to keep the lungs open.

 

Option C. Total Lung Capacity (TLC): Incorrect, because at TLC, airway pressure is positive, due to increased elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall.

 

Option D. Inspiratory Capacity (IC): Incorrect, because IC includes inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) and tidal volume (TV), both of which have positive airway pressures.

 

Educational Objective:

 

At Functional Residual Capacity (FRC), airway pressure is zero because lung recoil and chest wall expansion forces are balanced, making it the equilibrium point of the respiratory system.

questions.stem: Which of the following hormones act via JAK- STAT pathway?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Leptin

 

The JAK-STAT (Janus Kinase - Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription) pathway is a key intracellular signaling mechanism used by cytokines, growth factors, and certain hormones that bind to non-receptor tyrosine kinase-associated receptors.

 

  • Leptin acts via the JAK-STAT pathway.
    • Leptin binds to its receptor (LEPR), which activates JAK kinase.
    • This leads to STAT phosphorylation and translocation to the nucleus, where it regulates gene transcription related to appetite suppression and energy metabolism.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Aldosterone: Incorrect, because aldosterone acts via intracellular nuclear receptors (mineralocorticoid receptor), not JAK-STAT.

 

Option C. Oxytocin: Incorrect, because oxytocin acts via G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) using the IP₃-DAG pathway, not JAK-STAT.

 

Option D. Vitamin D: Incorrect, because Vitamin D binds to nuclear receptors (Vitamin D receptor, VDR), which function as ligand-activated transcription factors, not through the JAK-STAT pathway.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hormones that use the JAK-STAT pathway include Leptin, Growth Hormone, Prolactin, Erythropoietin, and Cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IFN-γ).

questions.stem: Which among the following has the highest airway resistance?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Bronchi

 

Airway resistance is determined by Poiseuille’s Law, which states that resistance (R) is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius (r⁴). This means that smaller airways have higher individual resistance, but their overall resistance is lower due to parallel branching.

 

  • Highest airway resistance is found in mid-sized airways, particularly the bronchi (segmental bronchi).
  • Although small bronchioles have a smaller diameter, they are highly branched and arranged in parallel, reducing their overall resistance.

 

Airway Resistance Distribution:

 

  1. Trachea – Moderate resistance.
  2. Large Bronchi (Primary & Secondary Bronchi) – Highest resistance due to moderate diameter and fewer branches.
  3. Small Bronchi & Bronchioles – Resistance starts decreasing due to increased branching and parallel arrangement.
  4. Respiratory Bronchioles & Alveolar Ducts – Lowest resistance because of large cross-sectional area.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alveolar duct: Incorrect, because these structures are highly branched and have very low resistance.

 

Option C. Respiratory bronchioles: Incorrect, because resistance is already significantly reduced in this region due to increased branching.

 

Option D. Small bronchioles: Incorrect, as they are highly branched, leading to less overall resistance despite their small diameter.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Mid-sized bronchi (segmental bronchi) have the highest airway resistance due to their moderate diameter and fewer branches.
  • Smaller bronchioles have less resistance because they are arranged in parallel, increasing the total cross-sectional area.

questions.stem: If the contractility of the heart is decreased, which of the following is seen? ESV: End-systolic volume EDV: End-diastolic volume

options.text: End diastolic volume and pressure curve shifts to left without change in slope

options.label: B
options.text: Slope changes in ESV pressure curve

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Slope changes in EDV and pressure curve

questions.answerText: Slope changes in ESV pressure curve
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Slope changes in ESV pressure curve

 

  • Contractility refers to the heart's ability to pump blood effectively.
  • When contractility decreases, less blood is ejected during systole, leading to:
    • Increased end-systolic volume (ESV) (more blood remains in the ventricle after contraction).
    • Decreased stroke volume (SV = EDV - ESV).
    • Rightward shift in the ESV pressure-volume curve because the heart is unable to generate as much force.
    • Change in the slope of the ESV pressure curve, indicating reduced contractile function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. End diastolic volume and pressure curve shifts to left without change in slope: Incorrect. A leftward shift in the EDV curve would indicate increased contractility, not decreased.

 

Option C. End systolic volume and pressure curve shifts to left without change in slope: Incorrect. Decreased contractility causes a rightward shift in the ESV curve, not left.

 

Option D. Slope changes in EDV and pressure curve: Incorrect. The EDV curve remains largely unchanged, as contractility affects ESV more than EDV.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Decreased contractility leads to increased end-systolic volume (ESV), decreased stroke volume (SV), and a rightward shift in the ESV pressure curve, with a change in slope.

questions.stemHtml: Researcher was studying the effect of hypoxia, hypercapnia and change in pH on ventilation, when he simulated the condition of hypoxia and hypercapnia with pH of 7.35 and plotted the graph, which one of the following is the appropriate representation of the given condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
">Ans. B) B

 

Explanation:

 

The given question involves hypoxia and hypercapnia with a slightly acidic pH of 7.35. The graph represents the relationship between alveolar PCO₂ and ventilation rate. In conditions of both hypoxia (low oxygen) and hypercapnia (high CO₂), the body responds by increasing ventilation to compensate for decreased oxygen and rising CO₂ levels.

 

Option B represents a moderate increase in ventilation, which is characteristic of the body's response to combined hypoxia and hypercapnia. In this state, ventilation increases to expel excess CO₂ while attempting to enhance oxygen uptake. The leftward shift and increased slope of the curve labeled B correspond to this physiological response.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Represents a normal ventilatory response to hypercapnia without the influence of hypoxia. The curve shifts to the right with increasing PCO₂, but the ventilatory increase is less pronounced compared to hypoxic conditions.

 

Option C: Likely represents a condition with either isolated metabolic acidosis or mild hypoxia but does not correspond to the expected response of combined hypoxia and hypercapnia.

 

Option D: Shows a more exaggerated ventilatory response seen in severe anemic hypoxia rather than the expected response to combined hypoxia and hypercapnia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The ventilatory response is significantly increased in hypoxia and hypercapnia due to the inability to efficiently expel CO₂ and maintain oxygenation. Understanding the different types of hypoxia and their effects on respiration is crucial in physiology and clinical medicine.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient visits a neurologist with a unique concern. The patient reports having difficulty recognizing familiar faces, including those of close family members and friends. This issue has been causing significant social discomfort. Which of the following conditions best describes the patient's symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Prosopagnosia

 

  • Prosopagnosia (also known as face blindness) is a neurological disorder characterized by the inability to recognize faces, even of close family members and friends.
  • This condition results from damage or dysfunction in the fusiform gyrus, specifically in the fusiform face area (FFA) of the inferior temporal lobe.
  • Patients with prosopagnosia can still recognize people by other cues (e.g., voice, clothing), but face recognition is impaired.
  • It is not related to memory loss or psychiatric disorders but is a specific defect in facial processing.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alzheimer’s disease 

 

  • Alzheimer's primarily affects memory and cognitive function, but it does not specifically impair face recognition in the early stages.
  • In later stages, it may cause generalized recognition difficulties, but prosopagnosia is distinct from dementia-related recognition issues.

 

Option C. Schizophrenia 

 

  • Schizophrenia is a psychiatric disorder that can lead to delusions, hallucinations, and cognitive impairment, but it does not primarily cause face recognition deficits.

 

Option D. Bipolar disorder: 

 

  • Bipolar disorder is characterized by mood disturbances (mania and depression) and does not impair face recognition.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Prosopagnosia is a neurological disorder caused by damage to the fusiform gyrus, leading to difficulty in recognizing faces while other visual and cognitive abilities remain intact.

questions.stem: Statement A: The Broca’s area will be localized in the parietal lobe of the cerebral cortex Statement B: The plan and motor patterns of word formation will be initiated at Broca’s area Which of the following is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The statement A is true, the statement B is false.

options.label: B
options.text: The statement A is false, the statement B is true.

options.label: C
options.text: Both the statements A and B are true

options.label: D
options.text: Both the statements A and B are false

questions.answerText: The statement A is false, the statement B is true.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) The statement A is false, the statement B is true.

 

  • Statement A:
    • Broca’s area is not localized in the parietal lobe; it is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the frontal lobe (usually in the left hemisphere).
    • The parietal lobe is primarily involved in sensory processing and spatial awareness, not speech production.
  • So statement A is false
  • Statement B is true:
    • Broca’s area is responsible for initiating the motor patterns of word formation, coordinating muscles involved in speech (tongue, lips, and vocal cords).
    • It plays a crucial role in speech production and articulation.
    • Damage to Broca’s area results in Broca’s aphasia, characterized by difficulty in speech production while comprehension remains intact.
  • So statement B is true

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Broca’s area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the frontal lobe, not the parietal lobe.
  • It is responsible for motor planning and execution of speech.
  • Broca’s aphasia causes difficulty in speech production but preserved comprehension.

questions.stem: Statement A: The lesion of lateral hypothalamus will result in anorexia Statement B: Hyperphagia is associated with the stimulation of ventromedial hypothalamus. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The statement A is true, the statement B is false

options.label: B
options.text: The statement A is false, the statement B is true

options.label: C
options.text: Both the statements A and B are true

options.label: D
options.text: Both the statements A and B are false

questions.answerText: The statement A is true, the statement B is false
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) The statement A is true, the statement B is false.

 

  1. Statement A is true:
    • The lateral hypothalamus is known as the hunger center.
    • It plays a crucial role in stimulating hunger and food intake.
    • A lesion in the lateral hypothalamus leads to anorexia and weight loss because the drive to eat is impaired.
  2. Statement B is false:
    • The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) is known as the satiety center.
    • Stimulation of the ventromedial hypothalamus leads to satiety, not hyperphagia.
    • However, a lesion in the ventromedial hypothalamus leads to hyperphagia (excessive eating) because the satiety signals are lost.
    • Since the question states stimulation (not lesion), the statement is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The lateral hypothalamus is the hunger center; its lesion leads to anorexia.
  • The ventromedial hypothalamus is the satiety center; its stimulation suppresses appetite, while its lesion causes hyperphagia.

questions.stem: The nigrostriatal projections to the striatum within the basal ganglia is associated with which neurotransmitter?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dopamine

 

  • The nigrostriatal pathway is one of the four major dopaminergic pathways in the brain.
  • It originates in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and projects to the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen).
  • This pathway plays a crucial role in motor control and movement regulation.

 

Clinical Significance:

 

  • Degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the nigrostriatal pathway is the primary cause of Parkinson’s disease, leading to resting tremors, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability.
  • Dopamine replacement therapy (e.g., L-DOPA) is used to manage Parkinson’s symptoms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glutamate: 

 

  • Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the corticostriatal pathway, but it is not the primary neurotransmitter of the nigrostriatal pathway.

 

Option B. GABA: 

 

  • GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the striatum and is involved in the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia.
  • However, it is not the neurotransmitter of the nigrostriatal pathway.

 

Option D. Acetylcholine: 

 

  • Acetylcholine plays a modulatory role in the basal ganglia but is not part of the nigrostriatal pathway.
  • Cholinergic interneurons in the striatum help regulate movement but function independently of the dopaminergic nigrostriatal projections.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The nigrostriatal pathway is a dopaminergic projection from the substantia nigra to the striatum and is essential for motor function. Degeneration of this pathway leads to Parkinson’s disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the major components of the Papez circuit? HippocampusMamillary bodyPrefrontal gyrusPineal gland
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1, 2

 

The Papez circuit is a neural pathway involved in the regulation of emotions and memory processing, particularly in the limbic system. It plays a crucial role in converting short-term memories into long-term memories.

 

The major components of the Papez circuit include:

 

  • Hippocampus (involved in memory formation)
  • Fornix (connects hippocampus to the mammillary bodies)
  • Mammillary bodies (relay station to the thalamus)
  • Anterior thalamic nuclei (relays information to the cingulate gyrus)
  • Cingulate gyrus (associated with emotional processing and memory retrieval)
  • Parahippocampal gyrus and Entorhinal cortex (help process and relay information to the hippocampus)

 

Other Options:

 

3. Prefrontal gyrus: Incorrect. The prefrontal cortex is involved in executive function and decision-making, not a primary component of the Papez circuit.

 

4. Pineal gland: Incorrect. The pineal gland is primarily responsible for melatonin production and circadian rhythm regulation, not for memory and emotions.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Papez circuit is a key limbic pathway that connects the hippocampus, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, and cingulate gyrus, facilitating memory formation and emotional processing.

questions.stem: Statement A: The deep and visceral pain are better localized compared to the superficial pain Statement B: There will be a deficiency of A delta fibers in the deep structures compared to superficial structures. Which of the following is correct?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.text: Both the statements A and B are true

questions.answerText: The statement A is false, the statement B is true
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) The statement A is false, the statement B is true

 

1. Statement A: The deep and visceral pain are better localized compared to the superficial pain:

 

  • Deep and visceral pain are poorly localized compared to superficial pain.
  • Superficial pain (from skin, mucosa) is sharply localized due to the presence of A delta fibers, which conduct pain signals rapidly and with precision.
  • Deep and visceral pain (from muscles, organs, and peritoneum) is dull, diffuse, and poorly localized due to the dominance of slow-conducting C fibers and the lack of specific pain receptors in visceral structures.
  • Visceral pain is often referred pain because of shared pathways in the spinal cord.

 

So statement A is false

 

2. Statement B: There will be a deficiency of A delta fibers in the deep structures compared to superficial structures.

 

  • A delta fibers are responsible for sharp, well-localized pain.
  • Deep structures and visceral organs have fewer A delta fibers compared to superficial structures.
  • Instead, they are primarily innervated by C fibers, which transmit slow, dull, and poorly localized pain sensations.
  • This explains why deep and visceral pain is more difficult to pinpoint compared to superficial pain.

 

So statement B is true

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Superficial pain is well-localized due to A delta fibers, while deep and visceral pain is poorly localized due to C fibers.
  • Deep and visceral structures have fewer A delta fibers, leading to dull and diffuse pain sensation.

questions.stem: The tactile discrimination will be affected in the lesion of this ascending sensory pathway of the spinal cord?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Posterior column

 

  • Tactile discrimination (fine touch, vibration, and proprioception) is mediated by the posterior column-medial lemniscus (PCML) pathway.
  • The posterior column (dorsal column) of the spinal cord contains two major tracts:
    • Fasciculus gracilis (lower limb)
    • Fasciculus cuneatus (upper limb)
  • These tracts carry fine touch, vibration sense, and proprioception to the brain.
  • A lesion in the posterior column results in loss of fine touch discrimination, vibration sense, and proprioception.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Spinothalamic tract: The spinothalamic tract carries pain, temperature, and crude touch but not fine touch discrimination.

 

Option C. Spinoreticular tract: The spinoreticular tract is involved in slow pain perception and autonomic responses to pain, not tactile discrimination.

 

Option D. Lateral lemniscus: The lateral lemniscus is part of the auditory pathway, not related to somatosensory transmission.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Fine touch, vibration, and proprioception are carried by the posterior column-medial lemniscus pathway.
  • Pain, temperature, and crude touch are carried by the spinothalamic tract.
  • Damage to the posterior column leads to loss of fine touch discrimination and proprioception.

questions.stem: In the lesion of fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus, which of the following sensations are expected to be affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Proprioceptors

 

  • The fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus are part of the posterior column-medial lemniscus (PCML) pathway, which is responsible for:
    • Fine touch (discriminative touch)
    • Vibration sense
    • Conscious proprioception (body position sense)
  • Fasciculus gracilis transmits sensations from the lower limb and lower trunk.
  • Fasciculus cuneatus transmits sensations from the upper limb and upper trunk.
  • A lesion in these tracts would impair proprioception, fine touch, and vibration sense.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pain sensations: Incorrect. Pain sensation is carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, not the posterior column.

 

Option B. Temperature sensations: Incorrect. Temperature sensation is also carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, not the posterior column.

 

Option D. All the above: Incorrect. Only proprioception, fine touch, and vibration are affected. Pain and temperature remain intact.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus are part of the posterior column-medial lemniscus pathway, which carries fine touch, proprioception, and vibration.
  • Pain and temperature sensations are transmitted via the lateral spinothalamic tract, not the posterior column.

questions.stem: All the following are types of mechanoreceptors, except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Taste buds 

 

  • Mechanoreceptors are sensory receptors that detect mechanical stimuli, such as pressure, stretch, vibration, and touch.
  • Taste buds, however, are chemoreceptors, meaning they respond to chemical stimuli (e.g., food molecules) rather than mechanical forces.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Muscle spindles – True mechanoreceptors: Detect muscle stretch and length changes, helping regulate muscle tone and reflexes.

 

Option B. Otolith hair cells – True mechanoreceptors:

 

  • Found in the vestibular system (utricle & saccule) of the inner ear.
  • Detect linear acceleration and head position changes by sensing movement of the otolith membrane.

 

Option D. Merkel cells – True mechanoreceptors: Located in the skin, responsible for light touch and pressure detection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Mechanoreceptors detect mechanical changes like pressure, vibration, and stretch.
  • Taste buds are chemoreceptors, responding to chemical stimuli, not mechanical stimuli.
